8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":17,"verseId":3,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Action and Fruit","totalVerses":33,"verseData":{"id":"v17_3","number":3,"title":"Intention Is Mental; Intentional Is Physical and Verbal","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"Of these, what is called 'intention' Is mental desire. What is called 'intentional' Comprises the physical and verbal."},"philosophy":{"insight":"Clarifying the distinction: intention (cetanā) = mental volition/desire (manas). Intentional actions = physical (kāya) and verbal (vāk) deeds. Mind → body/speech. The causal direction is from mental to physical, not vice versa.","madhyamaka":"Cetanā is mānasika (mental) — it's the mental factor of volition that initiates action. Cetayitvā karmāṇi are kāyika (bodily) and vācika (verbal) — the physical and verbal expressions of that mental volition. This threefold classification (mind, body, speech) is standard Buddhist analysis of karma.","quantum":"Wave function (potential/mental) → measurement outcome (actual/physical): the quantum state represents potential before measurement; the measurement outcome is the actual physical result. Mind→body parallels potential→actual.","bridge":"Both Buddhist karma and QM show a potential→actual structure. Buddhism: mental intention (potential) → physical/verbal action (actual). QM: wave function (potential) → measurement outcome (actual). Both: the invisible/mental precedes and shapes the visible/physical.","accessible":"Your thoughts and desires come first (intention). Then you act on them with your body and words (intentional). It's like an architect's design (mental) preceding the actual building (physical). The blueprint isn't the building, but the building follows from it.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, the mental→physical causal direction is real and ethically significant. Ultimately, mind, body, and speech are all empty — the distinction is conventional, not inherent.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying physical actions don't matter (only thoughts count). Physical/verbal actions ARE karma — but they're shaped by the underlying intention. Both matter; intention is primary."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Wave Function → Measurement Outcome","score":56,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"Wave function (potential) → measurement (actual) parallels intention (mental potential) → action (physical actual). The invisible precedes and shapes the visible.","caveat":"This is an analogy, not an identity. Wave functions are mathematical objects; intentions are mental experiences."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"A glowing mental intention transforming into physical movement (body) and sound waves (speech). The mental is the source; the physical/verbal are its expressions.","educationalGoal":"User sees the mental→physical causal direction in karma: intention first, then bodily and verbal expression."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why is the mental→physical direction important?","a":"It means ethics starts with the mind, not behavior. External compliance without internal change isn't true Dharma practice. You can follow all the rules externally while harboring malicious intent — and the karma reflects the intent.","realLifeExample":"Smiling at someone while secretly wishing them harm. The physical action (smile) is positive; the intention is negative. Buddhist karma weighs the intention more heavily."},{"q":"Are there three types of karma (mind, body, speech)?","a":"Yes — the standard threefold classification: (1) mānasika karma (mental actions — thoughts, attitudes), (2) kāyika karma (bodily actions), (3) vācika karma (verbal actions — speech). V.3 groups bodily and verbal under \"intentional\" and mental under \"intention.\"","realLifeExample":"Thinking angry thoughts (mental karma), hitting someone (bodily karma), and yelling at them (verbal karma) — three types, all rooted in the mental state of anger."},{"q":"How does \"mental desire\" relate to cetanā?","a":"Cetanā is the volitional mental factor — the \"urge\" or \"drive\" that directs consciousness toward an object and initiates action. It's not desire in the craving sense but volition in the directional sense — what you choose to attend to and act upon.","realLifeExample":"The moment before you reach for your phone — that's cetanā. Not the craving for information, but the volitional impulse that directs your hand. The volition that precedes and shapes the action."},{"q":"Does this mean we should only work on our minds?","a":"Both mind AND behavior matter. But mind is primary because: (1) mental karma is itself action, (2) physical/verbal actions follow from mental states, (3) changing the mind changes the behavior (but not always vice versa). Practice addresses all three levels.","realLifeExample":"An anger management course that only teaches physical restraint (don't hit) without addressing the mental anger isn't complete. The mind must change for lasting behavioral change."},{"q":"How does the wave function analogy work?","a":"A wave function describes what COULD happen (potential). Measurement reveals what DOES happen (actual). Similarly, intention describes what you WANT to do (potential). Physical/verbal action reveals what you DO (actual). Potential → actual in both cases.","realLifeExample":"A recipe (potential/intention) precedes the cooked dish (actual/action). The recipe shapes the dish. But the recipe isn't the dish — just as intention isn't the action."},{"q":"Why present these classifications (vv.2-5)?","a":"Nāgārjuna is establishing the conventional Buddhist framework of karma BEFORE analyzing it. By showing he understands the standard teaching, he demonstrates his critique isn't from ignorance but from deeper understanding. He accepts the conventions; he rejects only their inherent existence.","deeper":"VV.2-5 function as the \"thesis\" in a dialectical structure. Nāgārjuna presents the standard teaching (thesis), identifies its problems under inherent existence (antithesis, v.6), and resolves with emptiness (synthesis, vv.13-21). The dialectical movement is: convention → problem → resolution through emptiness."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"What is the relationship between intention and intentional actions?","options":["A) They're the same","B) Intention = mental volition (the source).
